title: Pandarus explains the failed shot
intro: The Trojans correctly suspect divine assistance but cannot see it as Diomedes can. Pandarus then explains why he came without horses. His account contrasts the well-provisioned household at home with the crowded conditions of the expedition.

notes.text: κοτεσσάμενος is aorist middle participle of κοτέομαι, ‘be angry,’ with dative Τρώεσσιν. μηνίσας is aorist active participle of μηνίω. ἱρῶν is genitive plural of ἱρόν, ‘sacrifice,’ giving the cause of resentment: a god may be angry over offerings. εἰ μή continues Aeneas’ reservation, ‘unless he is some god.’

ἔπι is adverbial, ‘is upon [us]’: the wrath of a god is hard to face. βουληφόρε is vocative of βουληφόρος, ‘counsel-bearing, counsellor,’ addressing Aeneas. χαλκοχιτώνων, ‘bronze-clad,’ agrees with genitive Τρώων; it means armoured men, not literal bronze undergarments.

ἐΐσκω means ‘liken, judge to resemble,’ with accusative μιν and dative Τυδεΐδῃ. πάντα is accusative of respect, ‘in every way.’ The datives ἀσπίδι and τρυφαλείῃ give the identifying equipment, shield and helmet. αὐλῶπις describes the helmet’s socket or tube, conventionally associated with the crest. σάφα means ‘clearly, for certain.’

μαίνεται is present middle of μαίνομαι, ‘rages’; τάδε is adverbial, ‘in this way.’ ἕστηκε is perfect of ἵστημι with present state, ‘stands.’ εἰλυμένος is perfect middle/passive participle of εἰλύω, ‘wrap’; ὤμους is accusative of respect, ‘wrapped about the shoulders,’ and νεφέλῃ the covering cloud. τις ἀθανάτων is partitive, ‘one of the immortals.’

κιχήμενον, from κίχημι / κιχάνω, describes the arrow reaching its mark. ἔτραπεν is second aorist of τρέπω, ‘turned’; ἄλλῃ is adverbial ‘elsewhere, aside.’ Pandarus infers interference from the nonfatal result. The narrator has already shown the wound and Athena’s help, allowing us to distinguish his inference from direct knowledge.

ἐφῆκα is first singular aorist of ἐφίημι, ‘I shot at him’; βάλον is first singular unaugmented aorist of βάλλω. προϊάψειν is future active infinitive of προϊάπτω, ‘send headlong,’ with dative Ἀϊδωνῆϊ, Hades. ἐφάμην, imperfect middle of φημί, introduces what he thought would happen. ἔμπης means ‘nevertheless.’

παρέασι is epic third plural of πάρειμι, ‘are at hand.’ τῶν is genitive after ἐπιβαίην, root-aorist optative of ἐπιβαίνω: ‘which I might mount.’ κεν makes the relative clause potential. πρωτοπαγεῖς and νεοτευχέες stress new construction, ‘fresh-built, newly made,’ of the eleven chariots at home.

πέπτανται is perfect middle/passive of πετάννυμι, ‘are spread,’ referring to coverings around the chariots. δίζυγες means paired for the yoke. ἑστᾶσι is perfect active of ἵστημι, ‘stand.’ ἐρεπτόμενοι, from ἐρέπτομαι, means ‘feeding on’; κρῖ is barley and ὄλυραι a cereal conventionally rendered spelt.

ἐπέτελλε is imperfect of ἐπιτέλλω, ‘enjoin,’ and ἐκέλευε restates the instruction. ἐμβεβαῶτα is epic accusative masculine singular perfect participle of ἐμβαίνω, describing the mounted state of με. ἀρχεύειν, present infinitive of ἀρχεύω, takes dative Τρώεσσι, ‘lead the Trojans.’ αἰχμητά is an epic masculine nominative, not a vocative here.

πιθόμην is unaugmented second-aorist middle of πείθω, ‘obeyed.’ ‘It would have been much better’ uses ἄν with past ἦεν, an epic imperfect of εἰμί. κέρδιον is comparative of κερδαλέος, ‘more advantageous.’ The unreal aside acknowledges that his practical calculation was wrong.

δευοίατο is epic third-plural optative of δεύομαι, ‘lack,’ after a verb of concern: ‘lest they lack fodder.’ εἰλομένων is aorist participle of εἴλω, ‘crowd together,’ in a genitive absolute with ἀνδρῶν. εἰωθότες is perfect participle of ἔθω, ‘accustomed,’ governing epic infinitive ἔδμεναι, ‘eat’; ἄδην means ‘to satiety.’ εἰλήλουθα is perfect of ἔρχομαι, ‘I have come.’
